summary:
When I discussed with @Jianlin_S , he said computing P^{-1/2} separately is unstable (context: Gram-NS; and that's why it needs restart) and I fully agree.
AND, he proposed an iterative method to compute P^{-1/2}G stably in
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKekaZabUAAdj8h.png
Quoting @kellerjordan0
I have some mixed feelings about this result:
On the one hand, it's genuinely impressive. I didn't know that Shampoo could be configured to perform this well on the benchmark.
On the other hand, the way this performance boost was achieved seems difficult to call "Vanilla," for the following reason:
According to @_arohan_, the boost depends upon fixing a numerical linear algebra issue that he observed to occur in my initial standard DistributedShampoo run. He fixed the issue by enabling the flag rank_deficient_stability_config=PseudoInverseConfig().
Here's the problem: This is an undocumented flag. It is contained within the 12,000-line DistributedShampoo codebase, but it does not appear in any user-facing documentation.
As a result, if someone tries to train a model using DistributedShampoo without either (a) knowing about this special undocumented flag or (b) being prepared to detect and fix the numerical linear algebra issues that may occur without it, then they won't be able to achieve @_arohan_'s level of Shampoo performance. This level of effort would be considered atypical for mere hyperparameter tuning.
--
[Note on Muon baseline in plot below: Rohan's post compared Shampoo to a slightly undertuned Muon baseline from 2026/05/01, which reached the target loss in 3375 steps. This resulted in a 50-step gap between Shampoo and Muon. In the figure below I'm using the up-to-date 2026/05/03 baseline, which reaches the target in 3325 steps. This results in the step-counts exactly matching between Muon and the tuned/stabilized Shampoo variant.]
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKd63AMbEAALzDx.jpg
clean_summary:
When discussing the stability of computing P^{-1/2} in Gram-NS, @YouJiacheng agrees with @Jianlin_S that calculating P^{-1/2} separately can be unstable and requires a restart. He proposes an iterative method to compute P^{-1/2}G more reliably, addressing numerical linear algebra issues that can arise during training.

A recent benchmark shows Shampoo achieving impressive performance, but this was partly due to enabling an undocumented flag, rank_deficient_stability_config=PseudoInverseConfig(), within the DistributedShampoo codebase. This flag is not documented and is necessary to attain the reported results, meaning users need to be aware of it to replicate the performance without encountering numerical issues. The updated results compare Shampoo to a Muon baseline, with the step counts aligning after stabilization.

> computing inverse roots is inherently more numerically unstable than orthogonalization
we can jointly compute inverse root and matmul (P^{-1/2}G) with an iteration, and it's more stable than P^{-1/2}.

Quoting @aurko79
As someone who watched Rohan train LLMs with shampoo and brainstorm ideas for making it cheaper/more scalable back in 2021-2022 (low-rank shampoo for very large weights etc), I think it's fair to say that Shampoo was certainly a step change over Adam.
That said Muon also introduced several innovations and it may be an over-simplification to say that it's just Shampoo with b2=0.
- For one the use of Nesterov momentum
- Second the observation that computing inverse roots is inherently more numerically unstable than orthogonalization
- Clever use of Newton-Schulz which makes it more GPU friendly than eigh or QR or coupled newton
- Scaling the update rms norm to match 0.2 (Adam update rms in the limit) which made grafting with Adam unnecessary
I think both optimizers are awesome and I learned a lot from studying both of them. Progress doesn't happen in a vacuum, we all stand on the shoulders of giants.

If stronger reasoning can be elicited through decoding alone, then a significant portion of reinforcement learning behavior may already be latent in the base model.

title: You Jiacheng (@YouJiacheng)
summary:
I have an alternative view based on the principle of symmetry and bi-orthogonal equivariance (Sections 3.2 & 3.8 of Not an attempt to attack Shampoo but just trying to understand the underlying geometric behavior of different optimizers.
Muon itself is an example of spectral optimizers such that whenever a matrix gradient or momentum direction is represented in a rotated basis (PGQᵀ or PMQᵀ for orthogonal P, Q), their update are transformed in the same way. Other instances also include Scion, PolarGrad and even vanilla SGD.
In contrast, in Section 3.8.1, it is shown that Shampoo (b2 != 0) is generally not a spectral operator of the current gradient/momentum alone, as the eigenvectors of L and R are not the same as the left and right singular vectors of G (or M). Since G (or M) is the (smoothed) steepest descent direction, any update map acts on it should preserve its singular vectors (i.e., a spectral operator). Ideally, the update map should preserve the update directions but potentially change the update magnitude of the directions, interpreted as some form of preconditioning.
Of course, there is gradient noise but I'd treat the M = EMA(G) as a denoiser rather than EMA(GGᵀ) or EMA(GᵀG). I think the so-called variance adaptation/damping (also in Adam) should rather be understood as an approximation of preconditioning, but such variance adaptation/damping isn't bi-orthogonal equivariant unless b2 = 0. Likewise, the elementwise variance-adaptation map in Adam is also not bi-orthogonal equivariant.
Following this argument, I would rather say that it boils down to determine the "best" spectral optimizer, i.e., the "best" absolutely symmetric map of the singular values of G (or M). Setting all singular values to one like in Muon might not be the best. I suspect that the "best" spectral optimizer might not exist and could be layer- or architecture-dependent, but there are some recent works on trying different powers of the singular values.
This is only my personal take and hope it would be constructive for developing a better understanding of the underlying behavior of different existing optimizers.

summary:

📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMPZA37boAAbnIv.jpg
Quoting @tikgiau
Introducing EdgeBench, a benchmark designed to study how agents learn from environments over at least 12~72-hour runs. We find that performance follows a log-sigmoid function of environment interaction time with high precision.
EdgeBench is built with three ingredients:
- 🌍 Real & Diverse: 134 real-world tasks across 6 task categories, spanning scientific problems, professional knowledge work, software engineering, optimization, formal math, and games.
- ⏳ Ultra-Long-Horizon: Each task supports 12–72 hours of agent work. Recorded human effort averages 57.2 hours.
- 🔁 Informative Feedback: Agents receive real-world feedback for continuous improvement.
After 38,000 hours of agent runs on EdgeBench, a scaling law for learning from environments emerges:
- 📈 As agents interact with task environments over time, their aggregate performance is precisely fit by a log-sigmoid function.
- 🧠 This phenomenon can be explained by an elegant theory of graph exploration.
We are releasing an initial 51 of the 134 tasks, together with the full evaluation framework, to help advance long-horizon agent research. Check our blog & paper for more findings!
